Finance and Accounting Automation: What to Automate From AP to the Financial Close

Finance teams spend half the week keying invoices, chasing approvals and reconciling accounts by hand, work that earns nothing and breaks the moment a number is wrong. Yet 79% of finance leaders say they need more automation, and only a third have started. Finance and accounting automation runs those cycles on their own, from procure-to-pay to the financial close. Here is what to automate, and where the judgment stays human.

Published by The Denzil Automations team

Updated 23 June 2026 · 15 min read

A finance team is hired to make sense of the numbers. Instead, most of its week goes to producing them by hand: keying invoices, chasing approvals and reconciling accounts line by line. More than half of a typical finance team's time disappears into that manual work, and it is error-prone by design, with an estimated 88% of the spreadsheets businesses still run on containing mistakes.

The will to change it is there; the action is not. Roughly 79% of finance leaders say they need more automation, while only about a third have made a meaningful start. A single invoice costs $16 to $22 to handle by hand, the close drags on for days, and the cost of waiting compounds month after month.

Finance and accounting automation closes that gap. It takes the repetitive work off the team so their hours go to analysis instead of admin, while the judgment that matters stays firmly with a person. The rest of this guide is a tour of where it fits: what to automate, the technology behind it, and the line you keep on the human side.

Finance runs on a few core cycles, and finance process automation slots into each one: procure-to-pay, order-to-cash and record-to-report, with treasury, tax and expenses around them. Here is what to automate in each, roughly in the order most teams should tackle them.

Procure-to-Pay: Invoices, Approvals and Payments

Procure-to-pay covers everything from raising a purchase order to paying the supplier, and it is where finance automation returns the most, fastest. Accounts payable automation captures each invoice with OCR and AI, matches it against the purchase order and receipt, routes it for approval and pays it, with no manual keying. The two-way and three-way match that once took an afternoon runs in seconds.

The numbers make the case on their own. A manual invoice costs $16 to $22 to process, and AP automation cuts that by up to 70% while catching the duplicates and fraud that slip past a tired reviewer. Despite this, only around 7% of finance teams have fully automated AP, which makes invoice automation one of the clearest wins still on the table.

Beyond the invoice itself, automation handles vendor onboarding, purchase-order creation, payment execution and AP reporting, closing the loop from request to payment. For a finance team drowning in supplier invoices, this is the cycle to automate first, and the one that pays for the rest.

Order-to-Cash: Billing, Collections and Cash

Order-to-cash is the mirror image: everything from a customer order to the cash in the bank. Accounts receivable automation, or AR automation, generates the invoice, sends it, chases payment with timed reminders and applies the cash when it arrives, so revenue is collected without a person nudging every account.

The slow, awkward part of AR is collections, and automation handles it without the friction. Dunning sequences escalate on their own, payment portals let customers pay in a click, and cash application matches incoming payments to open invoices. The result is faster cash and fewer overdue accounts, with the customer relationship intact, the same clean-data foundation behind any CRM automation.

Order entry and billing round out the cycle. Sales orders flow straight into the ledger, recurring invoices send themselves, and deductions and disputes route to the right person instead of stalling. For any business carrying receivables, automating order-to-cash turns a leaky, manual chase into a reliable inflow.

Record-to-Report: Reconciliation, the Close and Reporting

Record-to-report is the cycle that turns raw transactions into financial statements, and it is where manual work hurts most at month-end. Reconciliation automation matches ledger entries against bank and system data, flags only the exceptions, and posts the routine journal entries and day-to-day bookkeeping, so the books stay current instead of being rebuilt under deadline.

The financial close is the headline win, and financial close automation compresses a close that once took a week into a matter of days, with financial reporting running around 40% faster. Running this off live systems rather than a maze of spreadsheets is the same leap as moving from a spreadsheet to a live pipeline, applied to the ledger.

Reporting and revenue recognition complete the cycle. Financial reports build and distribute themselves on schedule, revenue is recognized against the rules, and fixed-asset and audit records update on their own. This is where robotic process automation in accounting earns its reputation, turning the most deadline-bound work in finance into a background process.

Reality check: the close is where automation is felt most. A team that closes in three days instead of ten gets a week of every month back for the work that moves the business forward.

Treasury and Cash Management

Around the three core cycles sits treasury, where automation brings visibility to cash. Bank statements consolidate into one view, cash positions and forecasts update in real time, and outgoing payments are validated against rules before they leave. Automated monitoring also watches for the unusual transaction that signals fraud, giving a finance lead a live picture of liquidity instead of a stale weekly spreadsheet.

Tax, Audit and Compliance

Tax and compliance run on rules and deadlines, which makes them a natural fit for automation. Tax codes are validated at the point of entry, filings and provisions are prepared on schedule, and a complete audit trail is kept without anyone assembling it by hand. When regulations such as SOX or local tax rules demand evidence, an automated, time-stamped record turns audit season from a scramble into a query.

Expense Management and Payroll

Two more processes round out the function. Automating expense management means receipts are captured from a photo, checked against policy and routed for approval and reimbursement, with the out-of-policy claims flagged rather than rubber-stamped. Payroll integration feeds hours and pay straight into the ledger, so the largest recurring cost books itself accurately every cycle.

The pattern: finance automation does not invent new work, it removes the keying and chasing between the numbers. The hours it gives back are the hours a finance team should spend on analysis, not data entry.

The Tech: RPA, AI and Agentic Automation

Three layers of technology do this work, and knowing which is which keeps expectations honest. Robotic process automation, or RPA in finance, runs the rules-based tasks: copying data between systems, matching invoices, posting routine entries. It is the workhorse behind most finance and accounting automation, predictable and cheap to run.

AI adds judgment where rules fall short. It reads a messy invoice, codes an unfamiliar expense, drafts a variance commentary and flags the anomaly a fixed rule would miss, which is where the recent leap in AI in business automation shows up in finance. Used together, RPA handles the volume and AI handles the exceptions.

Automation in the finance industry is moving from rules toward reasoning, and the newest layer is agentic automation, where AI agents coordinate a whole cycle end to end. An agent can run procure-to-pay or record-to-report from start to finish, handling exceptions and enforcing policy as it goes, lifting straight-through processing rates. It is promising and still maturing, so the sensible path is to automate the rules first, add AI to the exceptions, and let agents take the end-to-end work as they prove themselves.

Worth noting: most of the value in finance automation is still plain RPA, not AI. The rules-based matching and posting return more, and more reliably, than the cleverest model running on its own.

What Stays Human

Finance is accountable in a way few functions are, which sets a clear line on what to automate. The judgment calls, the forecasts and assumptions, the advice to the business and the response to an auditor's question, stay with a person. Automation prepares the numbers and surfaces the exceptions; a qualified human still reviews, signs and owns them.

The exceptions matter as much as the rules. A workflow handles the transactions that follow the pattern, but the unusual invoice, the disputed receivable and the year-end estimate need a human eye. Used this way, automation makes a finance team sharper and faster, because the freed hours go to the analysis and judgment that only people can provide, the same shift behind any serious business automation.

Where to Start, and What It Costs

Automating the whole function at once overwhelms a small team, so sequence it. Start with accounts payable and invoice processing, the highest-volume, fastest-payback cycle, then reconciliation and the close, then accounts receivable, and layer the rest on as each proves itself. Most finance teams feel the first win within a month.

The cost is within reach of a small business, not only an enterprise. Finance automation software runs as monthly subscriptions, and many automations bolt onto the accounting system or ERP you already run, from QuickBooks and Xero to NetSuite and Sage. Weighed against $16 to $22 per manual invoice and days of close time, the payback is usually quick and easy to show.

When the build spans several systems and the stakes are high, that is the point to weigh bringing in help. The trade-offs are the same ones we set out for choosing an automation agency, with the added requirement that whoever builds it understands accounting controls and the close.

Rule of thumb: automate the cycle that costs you the most hours first, which for most teams is accounts payable. Prove it on real invoices, then let the saving fund the next build.

Frequently Asked Questions

What can a finance team automate?

Almost any repeatable, rules-based task across the function: invoice capture and AP, billing and collections in AR, bank and ledger reconciliation, the financial close, reporting, expense management, payroll integration, tax validation and audit trails. The judgment, the forecasts and the sign-off stay with a qualified person. Most teams start with accounts payable, where the volume and payback are highest.

What is the difference between RPA, AI and agentic automation in finance?

They are three layers that work together. RPA runs rules-based tasks like matching and posting, AI adds judgment by reading messy documents and flagging anomalies, and agentic automation coordinates a whole cycle end to end. A sound approach automates the rules with RPA first, adds AI to the exceptions, then lets agents take on the end-to-end work as they prove reliable, a path we trace in our guide to AI agents versus chatbots.

How much does finance and accounting automation cost?

It runs as affordable monthly software subscriptions, and many tools extend the accounting system or ERP you already use rather than replacing it. Set against $16 to $22 per manually processed invoice and days of close time, the payback is usually fast. A done-for-you build adds a one-time setup fee, which a single automated cycle like AP often recovers within months.

What should we automate first?

Accounts payable and invoice processing, almost every time. It is the highest-volume, most error-prone cycle, and automating it delivers a clear, measurable saving quickly. From there, reconciliation and the financial close, then accounts receivable, are the natural next steps.

Will it work with QuickBooks, Xero or our ERP?

It should, and integration is the question that matters most. Good finance automation connects to the accounting system or ERP you already run, from QuickBooks and Xero to NetSuite, Sage and Microsoft Dynamics, using the connectors built for exactly that. Confirm that any tool or partner integrates with your stack before you commit.

Will automation replace accountants?

No. Automation takes the data entry, matching and chasing, while the analysis, judgment and advice that define the role stay with the accountant. In practice it makes finance professionals more valuable, by freeing them from the manual work to focus on the decisions the business genuinely needs.

Close the Books, Not the Day

A finance team's value is in the judgment: what the numbers mean, where the risk sits, what the business should do next. Everything around that, the keying, the matching, the chasing, the reconciling, is what should run on its own. Finance and accounting automation takes the manual cycle off the team so their hours go to the analysis only they can do.

Start with the invoices, automate one cycle, and let the saving prove itself before the next. That is the work we do for finance teams: the back-office cycles of procure-to-pay, order-to-cash and the close, automated cleanly and wired into the systems you already run, with the judgment and the sign-off left where they belong.
